data.text:
In a couple hours, Trump will impose a blockade on all maritime traffic entering and exiting Iranian ports. So why isn’t the market freaking out yet?

At first glance, Iran’s strategy to fight Trump by wreaking havoc on the global economy and making this war politically inconvenient is working.

A dozen countries, including big U.S. allies, are already in emergency mode.

For example, Australia’s industry is dealing with serious diesel shortages and is considering its own strategic stockpile bankrolled by the state.

Some European countries have only 8–10 days of jet fuel reserves left. And ACI EUROPE has formally requested emergency measures from the EU Commission DE.

Nations dependent on Middle Eastern crude, from the Philippines to India, are already rationing energy.

Even in the U.S., which is supposed to be insulated from the conflict given that it’s a net oil exporter, gas prices are at record highs and inflation posted its biggest monthly increase since 2022.

As a political third-order effect, some allies are turning to long-time adversaries to fix this. Spain’s PM flew to China today to convince Beijing to use its leverage to stop the war.

And yet, after this eventful weekend, the S&P 500 is set to open this morning just half a percent lower, with oil just over $100 a barrel as if nothing happened.

There are a few reasons why:
➡️ The blockade doesn’t change much. In its current state, the route is already close to impassable

➡️ George Boubouras of K2 Asset Management Ltd said on Bloomberg TV earlier that money managers are simply “looking through” this conflict. There’s so much bold rhetoric and political bluffing that it’s hard to take threats from either side at face value.

➡️ Wall Street is also buying the narrative that Trump has a much lower threshold for pain than the Iranians. “The Iranians, whatever happens, can sustain this for far longer than the world economy, far longer than the Gulf states, far longer than the Americans,” said Dr Andreas Krieg (@andreas_krieg), a senior lecturer at King's College London.

The good news is that both sides want a way out of this. The bad news is that the world needs oil while they’re looking for it.

Commentary by our editor @danrunk

data.text:
20,000 PEOPLE ARE BEING HELD HOSTAGE IN THE MIDDLE OF A WAR ZONE RIGHT NOW AND THE ENTIRE WORLD IS LOOKING THE OTHER WAY.

There are 2,000 ships sitting in the Persian Gulf right now that cannot leave.

On those ships are 20,000 human beings. Sailors. From the Philippines, India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh. Working class people who left their families to crew oil tankers and cargo vessels for a few hundred dollars a month.

They are the invisible workforce that keeps global trade moving.

They have been trapped for 45 days.

They watch missiles fly over their heads at night. They stay on deck because sleeping below feels like a coffin. 21 attacks on commercial vessels since this started. 10 sailors killed. An oil tanker hit by a sea drone 500 miles from the strait. A tugboat sunk by two missiles, three crew still missing.

"We don't sleep at night. We stay up on deck because you never know what might happen next."

That is a 28-year-old Indian sailor speaking to NBC from Iraqi waters minutes after an airstrike landed a few miles away.

The United Nations says there is no precedent for this situation since World War Two. The IMO declared a humanitarian emergency. The Secretary-General addressed 40 foreign ministers about it. 

And here is what changed: nothing.

Before this war, 150 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz every day. Now it is 4 or 5. The strait is mined. Iran lost track of some of its own mines. 

The US Navy is running clearance operations while Iran threatens to fire on those same ships. Two militaries operating in a 21-mile-wide waterway during a "ceasefire" that collapsed within six days.

And as of this morning, Trump declared a full naval blockade of the strait. Iran's Revolutionary Guard responded that any military vessel approaching will be "met with severe force."

Those 20,000 sailors are now caught between two blockades. Iran on the north side. The US Navy on the south. Trapped in a body of water that has become the most dangerous place on earth for a civilian to be, while the governments doing the blockading both claim they want the strait open.

The cruise passengers were evacuated. 15,000 of them got off six luxury liners weeks ago. The headlines covered that. Nobody covered the 20,000 who stayed because they are crew, not customers. They don't get evacuated. They get resupplied with food and water from Saudi Arabia and told to wait.

During COVID, these same sailors were confined to ships for months because of border restrictions. During the Red Sea crisis, they were attacked by Houthis. Nine killed. Eleven held captive for five months. Each time, the world forgot about them the moment the headlines moved on.

The pattern repeats because these people are invisible by design. They deliver the oil that heats your house and the goods that fill your shelves, and nobody thinks about them until the supply chain breaks.

Today, 20,000 of them are sitting in a war zone, between two navies, on top of sea mines, watching rockets at night, and the world is debating toll prices.

Remember them.
